source.title: Copiloting Diagnosis of Autism in Real Clinical Scenarios via LLMs
source.authors: Yi Jiang; Qingyang Shen; Shuzhong Lai; Shunyu Qi; Qian Zheng; Lin Yao; Yue-Ming Wang; Gang Pan

record.tranche_reason: The study compares LLM task performance across model sizes and explicitly reports a medium-size peak as an anti-scaling example, challenging predictable downstream improvement with scale in this task.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates ADOS-2 scoring and classification, not held-out language-model pretraining loss or parameter/token/compute scaling laws. Its scale results bear on V6 only. Prompt ablations and fusion-method comparisons are not scale results. Table 4 includes a random baseline, recorded as a control.
record.test_reason: An ADOS-2 autism-scoring application paper, not a scaling study. Appendix G.3 and Table 4 compare off-the-shelf models of different sizes in two families (Qwen1.5 14b–110b; Mistral 7b, Mixtral 8x7b, 8x22b) on one downstream task. That bears only on V6, in a new clinical setting. It is T3 rather than T5: the 'anti-scaling' remark is an observation, not a targeted argument against V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. On this ADOS-2 scoring task, medium-sized Qwen1.5 and Mistral-family models give the lowest average MAE, which the authors call an anti-scaling example. They speculate that larger models are misled by transcription noise and smaller ones cannot understand the task. This is a side analysis in an appendix; the paper's main conclusion concerns the ADOS-Copilot framework.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates clinical diagnostic scoring and classification across existing LLMs; it does not reproduce pretraining-loss or compute-allocation measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size and language specialization are reported to affect performance. The study also reports prompt-setting effects, but does not connect those prompt ablations to a pretraining-loss scaling law.
record.problems: The evaluation uses 28 clinical samples. The scale comparisons are task-specific, and Figure 10's values are not stated in the text. The study does not evaluate held-out pretraining loss, compute budgets, or pretraining-loss prediction.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for classification metrics in Table 4 were included; the scale claim is assessed primarily through average MAE and the authors' explicit scale analysis in Appendix G.3, Figures 10(a)-(b).

untested.parts: Pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute: not measured.
Extrapolation of fitted laws: none fitted.
Shape at fixed parameter count: not studied.
Other modalities or regimes: not studied as scaling.
Predictability from pretraining loss. Any fitted trend; only 3–4 sizes per family.

missing.what: Classification metrics by size. Qwen1.5 binary F1: 14b 0.7503, 32b 0.7381, 72b 0.7714, 110b 0.5158. Ternary F1: 0.5943, 0.6969, 0.7204, 0.5262. The peak is at 72b, not 32b, and 110b drops sharply. Mistral binary F1: 0.5265, 0.6190, 0.6773, i.e. monotonic improvement.
Inconsistent values for qwen1.5-72b: average MAE 0.4756 in Table 3 vs 0.4968 in Table 4; the text attributes 0.4805 to 72b.

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence for V6. It rests on 28 clinical samples with no uncertainty. The comparison covers 3–4 off-the-shelf checkpoints per family, which differ in more than size; Mixtral is MoE. A single prompt was used, ablated on Qwen1.5-32b. MAE is computed on 0–3 item scores. The direction differs between MAE and classification F1. Table values are internally inconsistent for the 72b model.

rows.subject: Qwen1.5 series
rows.operation_detail: Compared average MAE across model sizes in the series.

conditions.value: ADOS-2 M3 scoring; average MAE over eight items

rows.value: Figure only; the text states that medium-sized models perform best.
rows.note: The authors describe this as an anti-scaling example; figure values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Figure-only row that duplicates the Table 4 Qwen1.5 values (r3–r6). The pattern is an inverted U, not a simple reversal. MAE falls from 14b (0.5533) to 32b (0.4805), then rises at 72b (0.4968) and 110b (0.5179). Reversed holds only above 32b.

rows.operation_detail: Compared average MAE across model sizes in the series.

conditions.value: ADOS-2 M3 scoring; average MAE over eight items

rows.value: Figure only; the text states that medium-sized models perform best.
rows.note: The authors describe this as an anti-scaling example; figure values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Figure-only row that duplicates the Table 4 Mistral values (r7–r9). MAE improves from 7b (0.6526) to 8x7b (0.5649), then worsens at 8x22b (0.6786). Reversed holds only at the largest size. The Mixtral sizes are MoE models, so total vs active parameters confounds 'size'.

rows.subject: qwen1.5-110b
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated ADOS-2 scoring using the study's in-context enhancement prompt.
rows.note: Lower MAE is better; this individual value does not by itself establish a scale trend.
rows.check: Largest Qwen1.5 model, MAE 0.5179. Worse than 72b (0.4968) and 32b (0.4805). Lower MAE is better.

relationships.condition: Above medium size in each family: Qwen1.5 32b→72b→110b; Mixtral 8x7b→8x22b; ADOS-2 M3 average MAE
relationships.reason: Average MAE rises with size past the medium model: Qwen 0.4805→0.4968→0.5179; Mistral 0.5649→0.6786. Authors call this anti-scaling (r1, r2, r3, r4, r5, r7, r8).
relationships.display_finding: Average MAE rose from 0.4805 to 0.4968 to 0.5179 for Qwen1.5 and from 0.5649 to 0.6786 for Mixtral beyond the medium models.

relationships.condition: Small-to-medium sizes, and overall dependence on metric, prompt and sample
relationships.reason: MAE improves from small to medium (14b 0.5533→32b 0.4805; 7b 0.6526→8x7b 0.5649), giving an inverted U (r5, r6, r8, r9). The prompt was tuned on 32b, n=28, and no uncertainty is reported. Per the text, binary F1 instead peaks at 72b.
relationships.display_finding: MAE fell from 0.5533 at 14b to 0.4805 at 32b and from 0.6526 at 7b to 0.5649 at 8x7b, contributing to an inverted-U pattern, while binary F1 peaked at 72b; the prompt was tuned on 32b using 28 examples, without reported uncertainty.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Qwen1.5 and Mistral model-size comparisons on ADOS-2 scoring
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that medium-sized models perform best and call the result an anti-scaling example; the reported series comparison is not a predictable monotonic improvement with scale (r1-r2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The 32b model's average MAE of 0.4805 is lower than the 72b model's 0.4968 and the 110b model's 0.5179, but this task-specific comparison does not establish a general downstream scaling law (r3-r6).
